title: Federal aid can reach more places through state delivery while becoming harder to see and protect
source_unit: GAO-26-109100, Combating Fraud: Managing Risks in Federally Funded, State-Administered Programs, reissued with revisions August 7, 2026
geography: United States; federally funded programs administered by states and other nonfederal entities

observations.period: FY2025 program obligations; fraud-loss estimate based on FY2018–2022 data; report July 2026, revised August 2026

denominator.unit: selected large federally funded programs administered by states and other government entities; among 203 programs with obligations above $100 million

federal_obligations.value: about $1.1 trillion, nearly 90% of obligations among the qualifying programs
federal_obligations.unit: FY2025 federal obligations for the 20 selected programs

delivery_layers.value: funds may pass from federal agencies through states to subrecipients, contractors, subcontractors, Tribes, territories, local governments, or other entities

risk_assessment_documentation.value: 5 of 20 programs documented evidence consistent with identifying and assessing fraud risks to prioritize action; 15 did not

open_recommendations.unit: open GAO recommendations related to fraud-risk management among reviewed programs

government_wide_fraud_estimate.value: $233 billion to $521 billion annually, or 3% to 7% of average federal obligations
government_wide_fraud_estimate.unit: GAO estimate based on FY2018–2022 government-wide data, not a loss estimate for the 20 selected programs

recipient_outcome.value: not measured as a linked person- or household-level route from eligibility or payment through fraud exposure, remedy, service continuity, and later trust

observations.method: GAO used USAspending.gov FY2025 data to select 20 large programs, reviewed agency and program documents, GAO, Congressional Research Service, Inspector General, state-audit, and Department of Justice materials, and compared practices with fraud-risk frameworks and research. The review describes administration, oversight, identified risks, cases, and controls; it does not pool a common beneficiary outcome.
observations.uncertainty: The 20 programs are selected for size and are not a random sample. The $1.1 trillion obligation total is not money received by households, and the government-wide fraud range is not an estimate of losses in these programs. Missing risk assessments do not prove that a program had more fraud, and open recommendations do not prove that controls failed or losses occurred.
observations.subgroup: Federal agencies, states, Tribes, territories, local governments, subrecipients, contractors, beneficiaries, and taxpayers; program structures and legal oversight relationships differ.
observations.counterinterpretation: Decentralized delivery can be useful because state and local entities may know local needs and can prioritize projects. Multiple delivery partners can expand reach and specialized capacity. A documented risk assessment is not the same as effective fraud prevention, and a missing assessment may reflect documentation or timing rather than realized loss.

related_sources.claim: Official GAO report provides the program selection, obligation total, delivery layers, risk-assessment counts, examples, and open recommendations.
Earlier GAO fraud-risk review supplies broader recommendation and public-trust context but is not pooled with this 20-program observation.

boundary: This record adds a public-systems visibility layer: federal aid can be delivered through flexible state and local networks while oversight becomes more distributed. It does not estimate program-specific fraud prevalence, beneficiary loss, service denial, recovery, or public-trust change.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official GAO landing page and full report PDF reviewed; underlying USAspending.gov extract and program records are not retained.
